newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco divestment advocates see progress in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco divestment advocates see progress in 1997.

text.p: Groups that advocate divesting holdings in the tobacco industry said Thursday they saw greater interest in the movement and predicted that 1997 would be a turning point for institutional investors.
So far, there has been limited divestment involving some church groups, a small fraction of mutual funds, a few big state pension funds and universities.

But the advocacy groups, including "socially responsible" investment organisations and the American Medical Association, told reporters that divestment was being actively considered by a growing number of institutional investors concerned by both the ethics and the financial outlook for the industry.
The groups advocate divestment or other modifications such as reducing tobacco exposure or offering some tobacco-free alternative funds for investors.

Since the AMA called last June for health and life insurance companies to divest tobacco stocks and bonds, "we have received assurances from many" that they will begin pursuing such policies, AMA spokesman Dan Maier said in a conference call.
In addition, he said, "tens of thousands" of health professionals have downloaded disinvestment advice from the AMA's Website on the Internet, he said.

Alisa Gravitz, vice president of the Social Investment Forum and executive director of Co-op America, both of which advocate tobacco divestment, said, "We get calls all the time from the pension funds."
She said the funds, including some from states suing tobacco companies, have asked for confidentiality while they decide how to proceed.
"It is under serious debate around the country and that's what gives us this confidence" to predict that institutional investors will be forced to reconsider their portfolios in 1997, she said.
The advocacy groups also noted that there were 47 tobacco-related shareholder resolutions proposed last year, up from 15 in 1994.
Although many of them failed, the groups noted that it often takes several attempts to win support for such measures and that these initiatives were picking up steam.
The Maryland and New York state pension systems have already begun reducing their investment exposure to tobacco stocks and bonds.
The Social Investment Forum released a guide to disinvestment and other ways of reducing tobacco exposure. The group can be reached at 202-872-5319 or via the Internet at www.socialinvest.org.
